issues.legal_issue: A governmental order made under a statutory provision declared unconstitutional has no legal effect when that provision has not been reenacted, even if the constitutional basis for its invalidation is later removed.
material_facts: The government allowed an application to retain a disputed house by making an order under a statutory provision.
The Supreme Court had declared that provision unconstitutional and struck it down before the appeal was decided.
The provision had not been reenacted after the constitutional provision on which its invalidation was based was repealed.
The affected claimants challenged the government order, and the only ground raised in the appeal was that the order rested on the invalidated provision.
issues.conclusion: The government order was illegal and invalid and could have no effect; the Court set it aside along with the High Court judgment that had declined to interfere with it.
issues.legal_principle: In Lachhman Dass and Ors. v. Municipal Committee, Jalalabad and Ors., the Court held Section 20-B of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 ultra vires Article 31(2) of the Constitution. Although Article 31(2) was later repealed by the Constitution (Forty-Fourth Amendment) Act, 1978, Section 20-B was not reenacted. An order made under that unconstitutional provision could not be given effect.

predicates.appeal_challenges_government_order: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a government order.
predicates.order_rests_on_invalidated_provision: The government made the challenged order under a provision that a court had declared unconstitutional.
predicates.provision_not_reenacted: The provision had not been reenacted after the constitutional basis for its invalidation was removed.

issues.definition: If an appeal challenges a government order made under a provision declared unconstitutional and that provision was not reenacted, the order has no legal effect.
